title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Contents


Part 1: Dataset Overview

About the data
Key variables and derived metrics

Part 2: Portfolio Composition

Policy and geographic breakdown
Driver and vehicle profile


Part 3: Profitability Analysis

Loss ratio distributions
Key drivers of profitability

Part 4: Volatility Analysis

Claim frequency patterns
Geographic and temporal effects



Good morning everyone. Today I will be walking you through an exploratory visual analysis of a real motor insurance portfolio from Spain. The dataset covers three years of policy transactions and gives us a great opportunity to look at what actually drives profitability and claims volatility. We will move through four parts: dataset overview, portfolio composition, profitability analysis, and volatility analysis.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
About the Dataset


Source: Spanish motor insurer microdata
Period: January 2022 – December 2024
Records: 354,140 policy transactions
Variables: 47 across 4 groups



Group
Variables




Policy & Insured
8


Driver & Vehicle
10


Premiums
8


Claims & Incurred
21




Three derived metrics guide analysis:
\[\text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Incurred}}{\text{Premium}}\]
\[\text{Claim Freq} = \frac{\text{Claims}}{\text{Exposure}}\]
\[\text{Severity} = \frac{\text{Incurred}}{\text{Claims}}\]






Note


Loss Ratio < 1 = Profitable
Loss Ratio > 1 = Unprofitable





This is real anonymised data from a Spanish motor insurer. Each row is one policy in one year. Loss ratio is our profitability measure — below 1 means profitable. Claim frequency tells us how often accidents happen per year of exposure. Severity tells us the average cost per claim when one does occur.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Data Quality


fuel_type: 0.37% missing — excluded when fuel type is analysed
vehicle_value: 0.14% missing — excluded when vehicle value is analysed
All remaining 45 variables are 100% complete


Only two of 47 variables have any missing values at all. Fuel type is missing for 0.37 percent and vehicle value for 0.14 percent. Both are handled by exclusion. Everything else is complete, which is exceptional for a real-world dataset of this size.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Policy Type Distribution


Looking at what the portfolio is made of, CC policies dominate at 58 percent. These are third-party liability combined with several add-ons like theft and glass. COMP_E at 26 percent is full comprehensive with an excess. TPG comes in at 10 percent. What stands out is how rare basic TP policies are at just 1.6 percent. This tells us the insurer is largely serving customers who want broader protection.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Policy Status & Bonus Score


On the left, 89 percent of policies are active and 11 percent cancelled. That cancellation rate is worth noting as mid-term cancellations reduce premium income. On the right, the bonus score breakdown shows 96 percent of customers have a Good score, meaning they have had no recent claims. This is very positive for profitability but it also means the Bad group at just 1.3 percent and Neutral at 2.2 percent are so small we need to be careful drawing conclusions from them.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Driver Age & Vehicle Profile


Three things jump out from these charts. First, the typical driver here is in their mid-40s to mid-50s. Very few young drivers under 25 appear in this book, likely because premiums for that age group are too high. Second, the vehicles are quite old, with many in the 15 to 35 year range. Third, vehicle values mostly sit between 15 and 40 thousand euros. We capped the vehicle value chart at 80k to show the actual shape of the distribution.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Geographic Distribution


The geographic mix shows inland as the dominant segment at 65 percent, coastal at 29 percent and islands at 7 percent. Urban circulation edges ahead of rural at 54 versus 46 percent. Diesel vehicles make up 64 percent of the fleet, though this may shift as newer petrol and electric vehicles gain market share in coming years.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Loss Ratio Overview


I have split this into two panels to make the story clearer. On the left, 88 percent of policies never filed a single claim. On the right, we look only at the claimants. Even among those who did claim, most had a loss ratio below 1, meaning premiums still covered the cost. But there is a meaningful tail beyond break-even. These are the policies driving all the losses. The chart is capped at 3 because the tiny number of extreme outliers beyond that just stretches the axis without adding insight.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Loss Ratio by Policy Type


Now we can see exactly how policy type shapes profitability. With the x-axis capped at 2, the distributional differences are finally visible. COMP_E and COMP_N sit at the top with the widest and most spread-out distributions. TP and TPG at the bottom are almost entirely at zero because they only cover third-party liability. CC sits in the middle. The key takeaway is that policy type is one of the clearest drivers of loss ratio.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Loss Ratio by Bonus Score


This is probably the most striking finding in the profitability section. With the y-axis capped at 1.5, we can now actually see the differences between groups. The Bad-score violin on the right is noticeably wider and taller than the Good group on the left. This confirms the bonus-malus system is working. It correctly identifies the riskier customers. Even though the Bad group is less than 1 percent of the portfolio, they contribute disproportionately to aggregate losses.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Claim Severity by Policy Type


Not only do comprehensive policies have more claims, but each claim also costs more. COMP_E and COMP_N show the highest severity distributions. That is because they cover events like total vehicle loss and theft, which are expensive. CC sits in the middle. What is also notable is how wide the spread is within each policy type. The interquartile range is huge across all types, which tells us that predicting how much any individual claim will cost is genuinely difficult.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Claim Frequency by Driver Age


This chart shows a pattern that actuaries know well. The youngest drivers from 19 to 25 have the highest claim frequency by a clear margin. Then it drops steadily through the middle age groups as drivers gain experience. It ticks back up slightly for drivers over 65. The U-shape is now clearly visible since we filtered out the NA group and scaled the y-axis appropriately. One note: the 19-25 bar is based on a small sample as very few young drivers appear in this portfolio.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Claim Frequency by Geography


Geography matters quite a bit for claim frequency. Urban drivers consistently file more claims than rural drivers across all three municipality types. That is not surprising given higher traffic density in cities. What is interesting is that island municipalities show the highest urban claim frequency of all. Coastal urban areas also come in elevated. So combining municipality type and circulation area together gives a more nuanced picture of geographic risk than either variable alone.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Loss Ratio Trend Over Time


Looking at the trend over three years gives us a sense of whether profitability is improving or getting worse. With the repelled labels on the left, we can now clearly read which line belongs to which policy type without the overlap. Comprehensive policies sit higher than basic ones throughout. What we want to watch for is any lines moving upward over time, as that could point to rising repair or medical costs squeezing margins.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Key Findings Summary


Profitability

🔵 COMP/N LR: 0.71 → 1.17 (2022-2024)
🔵 COMP/E LR: 0.64 → 1.11 (2022-2024)
⬜ Bad-score policyholders: IQR 0.31-1.05
⬜ 88.1% of policies have zero claims


Volatility

🔵 19-25 drivers: 0.716 claims/yr (2.5x vs safest group)
🔵 Inland Urban: 0.371 claims/yr (highest region)
⬜ Urban always > Rural across all municipality types
⬜ Wide severity IQR across all policy types








Important


Core finding: 88.1% of policies have zero claims. The portfolio’s challenge is that COMP/N and COMP/E (full comprehensive policies) have now crossed break-even — the insurer is losing money on these segments.




To summarise. The biggest story is the trend: COMP/N rose from 0.71 to 1.17 and COMP/E from 0.64 to 1.11 over three years. Both are now loss-making. On the volatility side, young drivers at 0.716 and inland urban areas at 0.371 are the highest-frequency segments. Young drivers file claims 2.5 times more than the 56-65 group. The overarching finding is that 88 percent of policies are fine. The challenge is managing the small but growing share of loss-making comprehensive policies.

Two graphs side by side

  ggtitle("English vs Maths scores")

  plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'I')

p3 + inset_element(p2, left = 0.02, bottom = 0.7, right = 0.5, top = 1)

text:
pacman::p_load(ggdist, ggridges, ggthemes,
               colorspace, tidyverse)





exam <- read_csv("data/Exam_data.csv")








The PlotThe Code














ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = lighten("#7097BB", .3),
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
    ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()








The PlotThe Code














ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS,
           fill = stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Temp. [F]",
                       option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()








The PlotThe Code














ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5-stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient", 
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()








The PlotThe Code














ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()








The PlotThe Code














ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)
    ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#FF0000A0", "#A0A0A0A0", "#0000FFA0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +
  theme_ridges()

       aes(x = RACE,

Funnel Plot with ggplot2

Computing Derived Fields

df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death / Positive) %>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate*(1-rate)) / (Positive))) %>%
  filter(rate > 0)

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1/df$rate.se^2)



Computing Confidence Interval Limits

number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
dfCI <- data.frame(number.ll95, number.ul95, number.ll999, 
                   number.ul999, number.seq, fit.mean)



Static Funnel Plot

The PlotThe Code














p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Positive, y = rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(label=`Sub-district`), 
             alpha=0.4) +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ll95), 
            size = 0.4, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ul95), 
            size = 0.4, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ll999), 
            size = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ul999), 
            size = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(data = dfCI, 
             aes(yintercept = fit.mean),

  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,0.05)) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = -0.13, label = "95%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") +

        legend.text = element_text(size=7),

panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits=2, prefix="", cex.cor, ...) {
  usr <- par("usr")
  on.exit(par(usr))
  par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
  r <- abs(cor(x, y, use="complete.obs"))
  txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits=digits)[1]
  txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep="")
  if(missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8/strwidth(txt)
  text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)
}

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics of Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Motor vehicle insurance is one of the largest lines of non-life (property & casualty) insurance globally. According to Swiss Re’s sigma research, non-life insurers face two fundamental challenges: maintaining profitability (ensuring premiums collected exceed claims paid) and managing volatility (the unpredictable nature of claim occurrences and severities).
This exercise analyses a detailed microdata portfolio from a Spanish motor insurance company, covering 354,140 policy transactions from January 2022 to December 2024 across 47 variables. The dataset captures policy characteristics, driver and vehicle attributes, premiums charged, and claims experience.



Using Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) methods and ggplot2 visualisations, this exercise explores:

Univariate distributions of all numerical and categorical variables
Bivariate relationships to statistically identify factors influencing profitability and volatility




Two derived metrics guide the analysis throughout:

Loss Ratio = total_incurred / total_premium: the primary measure of profitability. A loss ratio below 1 indicates the insurer collected more in premiums than it paid in claims.
Claim Frequency = total_claims / total_exposure: measures how often claims occur per policy year, a key driver of volatility.
Claim Severity = total_incurred / total_claims (where claims > 0): the average cost per claim.

         policy_type = fct_reorder(policy_type, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_type, y = n, fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct * 100, 1), "%")),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "TP"     = "#BBDEFB", "TPG" = "#90CAF9",
    "CC"     = "#42A5F5", "COMP_E" = "#1976D2",

  labs(title = "Distribution of Policy Type",
       x = NULL, y = "Number of Policies") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())









Observation: The CC policy type dominates the portfolio at over 62%, followed by COMP_E at around 22%. The basic TP policies are rare at under 1%, suggesting this portfolio skews toward customers who elect broader coverage. The near-absence of basic TP policies may indicate a deliberate underwriting strategy targeting higher-coverage segments.



3.2 Distribution of Policy Status

Observation: Approximately 85% of policies are active and 15% cancelled. The cancellation rate of 15% is not negligible. Policies cancelled mid-term reduce premium income and may signal adverse selection if higher-risk customers are disproportionately cancelling after claims.



3.3 Distribution of Business Type, Payment Frequency, and Bonus Score


Show the code

Annual payment is overwhelmingly preferred (78%), likely reflecting discounts offered for upfront payment. The bonus score distribution is highly skewed toward “Good” (98%), indicating the portfolio is dominated by low-risk, experienced drivers with no recent claims history.

  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio, y = policy_type, fill = policy_type)) +

Observation: Loss ratio distributions vary markedly across policy types. Comprehensive policies (COMP_E and COMP_N) show the widest distributions and highest medians, reflecting the broader coverage they provide. The TP and TPG policies are concentrated near zero as their coverage is limited to third-party liability only.



6.2 Loss Ratio by Bonus Score


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio), total_premium > 0,
         loss_ratio > 0, loss_ratio <= 1.5) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bonus_score, y = loss_ratio, fill = bonus_score)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE, trim = TRUE,
              colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA,
               show.legend = FALSE, fill = "white",
               colour = "#444444", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "#B71C1C",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 1.05,
           label = "Break-even (LR = 1)", hjust = 0,
           colour = "#B71C1C", size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Good"    = "#66BB6A",
                                "Neutral" = "#FFA726",

       x = "Bonus Score", y = "Loss Ratio",
       caption = "< 3% of claimants exceed LR = 1.5 and are excluded") +
  theme_minimal()









Observation: Policyholders with a “Bad” bonus score exhibit substantially higher median loss ratios and greater distributional spread compared to “Good” policyholders, confirming that the bonus-malus system successfully identifies high-risk customers. The “Bad” group contributes disproportionately to portfolio volatility despite representing less than 1% of policies.



6.3 Claim Frequency by Driver Age Group


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(claim_frequency), total_exposure > 0) |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(driver_age,
                          breaks = c(18, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 100),

                          right = TRUE)) |>

  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(mean_freq = mean(claim_frequency), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = mean_freq)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#42A5F5") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_freq, 3)),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.85)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(title = "Mean Claim Frequency by Driver Age Group",
       x = "Driver Age Group", y = "Mean Claim Frequency (claims/policy year)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())









Observation: Claim frequency is highest for the youngest driver age group (19–25), consistent with actuarial research on inexperienced drivers. Frequency gradually decreases for middle-aged drivers (35–55) and slightly increases again for older drivers (65+), forming a characteristic U-shape. This pattern justifies age-based premium differentiation.



6.4 Claim Frequency by Driving Experience Group


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(claim_frequency), total_exposure > 0,
         driving_experience >= 0, driving_experience <= 60) |>
  mutate(exp_group = cut(driving_experience,
                          breaks = c(-1, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 60),
                          labels = c("0-5", "6-10", "11-20",
                                     "21-30", "31-40", "41+"))) |>
  filter(!is.na(exp_group)) |>
  group_by(exp_group) |>
  summarise(mean_freq = mean(claim_frequency), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = exp_group, y = mean_freq)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#7E57C2", width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_freq, 3)),

  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +

       x = "Years of Driving Experience", y = "Mean Claim Frequency (claims/policy year)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())









Observation: Claim frequency decreases consistently as driving experience increases, with the least experienced drivers (0–5 years) showing the highest frequency. This pattern reinforces the driver age findings and confirms that experience, independent of age, is a meaningful risk predictor. The most experienced drivers (41+ years) show the lowest claim frequency, though this group also tends to be older.



6.5 Loss Ratio by Vehicle Age Group


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio), total_premium > 0,
         loss_ratio > 0, loss_ratio <= 1.5) |>
  mutate(veh_age_group = cut(vehicle_age,

             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues") +
  labs(title = "Loss Ratio by Vehicle Age Group",
       subtitle = "Claimants only (LR > 0), capped at 1.5",
       x = "Vehicle Age Group (years)", y = "Loss Ratio",
       caption = "< 3% of claimants exceed LR = 1.5 and are excluded") +
  theme_minimal()









Observation: Newer vehicles (0–5 years) show wider loss ratio distributions, possibly driven by higher repair costs or declared values. Very old vehicles (31+ years) show lower and more concentrated loss ratios, likely because they carry lower insured values resulting in smaller absolute claim amounts.



6.6 Claim Severity by Policy Type


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(claim_severity), total_claims > 0) |>
  filter(claim_severity <= quantile(claim_severity, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_type, y = claim_severity, fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE, trim = TRUE,
              colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA,
               show.legend = FALSE, fill = "white",

  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Claim Severity by Policy Type",
       subtitle = "Capped at 99th percentile  |  Policies with claims only",
       x = "Policy Type", y = "Claim Severity (EUR per claim)") +
  theme_minimal()









Observation: Comprehensive policies (COMP_E and COMP_N) show substantially higher claim severity compared to basic coverage types, reflecting their broader protection against costly events like theft and total loss. High variance within each policy type highlights the difficulty of predicting individual claim costs.

  group_by(municipality_type, circulation_area) |>
  summarise(mean_freq = mean(claim_frequency), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = municipality_type, y = mean_freq,
             fill = circulation_area)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.75), width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_freq, 3)),
            position = position_dodge(0.75),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 3.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Urban" = "#42A5F5", "Rural" = "#66BB6A")) +
  labs(title = "Mean Claim Frequency by Municipality Type and Circulation Area",
       x = "Municipality Type", y = "Mean Claim Frequency",
       fill = "Circulation Area") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())









Observation: Urban circulation consistently shows higher claim frequencies than rural across all municipality types, consistent with greater traffic density and accident risk in urban environments. Island municipalities exhibit the highest urban claim frequencies. This geographic segmentation demonstrates that both location type and circulation environment are meaningful predictors of claim volatility.



7.2 Claim Frequency by Vehicle Brand (Top 12)


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(claim_frequency), total_exposure > 0) |>
  group_by(vehicle_brand) |>
  summarise(
    mean_freq = mean(claim_frequency),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n >= 500) |>
  slice_max(mean_freq, n = 12) |>
  mutate(vehicle_brand = fct_reorder(vehicle_brand, mean_freq)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = vehicle_brand, y = mean_freq, fill = mean_freq)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_freq, 3)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.2) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#90CAF9", high = "#1565C0") +
  labs(title = "Mean Claim Frequency by Vehicle Brand (Top 12)",
       subtitle = "Brands with at least 500 policies only",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean Claim Frequency (claims/policy year)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())









Observation: Claim frequency varies meaningfully across vehicle brands, indicating that brand is a relevant risk factor beyond what is captured by vehicle age and value alone. This variation may reflect differences in driver demographics, vehicle use patterns, or inherent vehicle safety characteristics across brands.



7.3 Loss Ratio Over Time (Year)


Show the code
trend_data <- insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio), total_premium > 0) |>
  group_by(year, policy_type) |>
  summarise(mean_lr = mean(loss_ratio), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(trend_data,
       aes(x = year, y = mean_lr,
           colour = policy_type, group = policy_type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#B71C1C", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = filter(trend_data, year == 2022),
    aes(label = paste0(policy_type, " ", round(mean_lr, 2))),
    direction   = "y",
    nudge_x     = -0.3,
    size        = 3,
    show.legend = FALSE,
    segment.color = "grey70",
    segment.size  = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2022, 2023, 2024),
                     expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 0.3))) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Mean Loss Ratio by Policy Type Over Time (2022-2024)",
       x = "Year", y = "Mean Loss Ratio", colour = "Policy Type") +
  theme_minimal()









Observation: Loss ratios vary across years and policy types. Comprehensive policies consistently sit above basic coverage types throughout the three-year period. Any upward trend could indicate inflationary pressure on claims costs such as rising repair or medical expenses.



7.4 Relationship Between Premium and Incurred Cost


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(total_incurred > 0, total_premium > 0) |>
  filter(total_premium  <= quantile(total_premium, 0.99),
         total_incurred <= quantile(total_incurred, 0.99)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_premium, y = total_incurred,
             colour = policy_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#B71C1C",
              linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Premium vs Incurred Cost (Policies with Claims)",
       subtitle = "Red dashed line = break-even (premium = incurred cost)",
       x = "Total Premium (EUR)", y = "Total Incurred (EUR)",
       colour = "Policy Type") +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 2)))









Observation: Most policies with claims fall below the break-even line (incurred < premium), indicating individual profitability. However, a notable cluster of policies exceed the break-even line, representing loss-making contracts. These tend to be clustered among comprehensive policies, confirming that wider coverage generates both higher revenue and higher claims exposure.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics of Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
8 Summary and Conclusion
This analysis explored the motor vehicle insurance portfolio across 354,140 policies spanning 2022–2024 using univariate and bivariate EDA methods. All 47 variables were examined across 5 EDA sections.
Key findings on profitability:

The portfolio is dominated by CC and COMP_E policy types which carry the highest claim severity
Bonus score (claims history) is a strong predictor of loss ratio. “Bad” policyholders show markedly higher and more variable loss ratios
Comprehensive policies (COMP_E, COMP_N) consistently exhibit higher loss ratios than basic coverage types
Over 88% of policies generate zero claims, creating a highly skewed loss distribution that drives average loss ratios

Key findings on volatility:

Young drivers (19–25) and drivers with less than 5 years of experience show the highest claim frequencies
Urban circulation and island municipalities show the highest claim frequencies across all regions
Vehicle age, municipality type and circulation area all contribute to claim frequency variation
Vehicle brand shows meaningful variation in claim frequency, indicating that brand is a risk factor beyond age and value alone
The heavy right tail in both claim frequency and severity distributions is the primary source of portfolio volatility

section: Insight 1: CC Policies Dominate the Portfolio
text:
Insight 1: CC Policies Dominate the Portfolio


CC (Third-party + add-ons) is the dominant policy at 57.8% of the portfolio
COMP_E (Comprehensive with excess) is second at 25.8%
Basic TP (Third-party only) is rare at just 1.6% — most customers prefer broader coverage


CC policies dominate at 58 percent. These are third-party liability combined with several add-ons like theft and glass. COMP_E at 26 percent is full comprehensive with an excess. What stands out is how rare basic TP policies are at just 1.6 percent. This tells us the insurer is largely serving customers who want broader protection.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 2: Portfolio is Stable with Low-Risk Customers
text:
Insight 2: Portfolio is Stable with Low-Risk Customers


89.2% of policies are active; cancellation rate of 10.8% warrants monitoring
96.4% of customers have a Good bonus score — no recent claims history
Bad-score customers are only 1.3% of the portfolio but are a key risk segment


On the left, 89 percent of policies are active and 11 percent cancelled. On the right, the bonus score is striking. 96 percent of customers have a Good score, meaning they have had no recent claims. This is very positive for profitability. But it also means the Bad group at 1.3 percent is very small so we need to be careful drawing conclusions from it statistically.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Insight 3: Experienced Drivers, Older Vehicles


Most drivers are aged 40-60 years — an experienced, lower-risk segment
Vehicle age peaks at 15-35 years — an older fleet than typical
Vehicle values concentrate between €15k-€40k with a high-value tail


Three things jump out from these charts. First, the typical driver here is in their mid-40s to mid-50s. Very few young drivers under 25 appear in this book. Second, the vehicles are quite old with many in the 15 to 35 year range. Third, vehicle values mostly sit between 15 and 40 thousand euros, but there are expensive vehicles in the tail that can generate very large claims.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Insight 4: Urban-Heavy, Inland-Dominant Portfolio


64.6% of policies are in inland municipalities; islands account for only 6.8%
Urban and rural circulation are split 53.8% vs 46.2% — near equal exposure
64.2% of vehicles use diesel — relevant for repair cost patterns


The geographic mix shows inland as the dominant segment at 65 percent. Urban and rural circulation are fairly balanced. Diesel vehicles make up 64 percent of the fleet. These splits matter because urban and rural drivers have very different claim frequencies as we will see shortly.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 5: 88% of Policies Have Zero Claims
text:
Insight 5: 88% of Policies Have Zero Claims


88.1% of policies generate zero claims; only 11.9% file any claim
Among claimants, the distribution peaks near LR = 0.1-0.3 and decays toward break-even
9.0% of all policies exceed break-even (LR > 1) — these drive total portfolio losses


I have split this into two panels. On the left, 88 percent of policies never filed a single claim. On the right, we look only at the claimants. The distribution peaks near 0.1 to 0.3 and decays toward the break-even line. Only 9 percent of all policies exceed break-even. These are the policies that really matter for the portfolio bottom line.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 6: Comprehensive Policies Have Higher Loss Ratios
text:
Insight 6: Comprehensive Policies Have Higher Loss Ratios


COMP/N: Full mean LR = 0.950, median = 0.897 — highest among all policy types
COMP/E: +Excess mean LR = 0.942, median = 0.915 — second highest
TP: Basic mean LR = 0.864, median = 0.676 — narrowest distribution, lowest loss ratio


This raincloud plot from Chapter 9 combines a half-density curve, boxplot, and mean diamond marker in one chart. The blue half-densities for COMP/E and COMP/N are visibly wider and taller than the grey ones. The mean diamond sits above the median box line for all types, showing the right-skew of insurance losses. Comprehensive policies have both higher medians and wider spreads.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 7: Bad Claims History Predicts Higher Loss Ratios
text:
Insight 7: Bad Claims History Predicts Higher Loss Ratios


Bad-score median LR = 0.668, IQR = 0.31–1.05 — wide spread crossing break-even
Good-score median LR = 0.724, IQR = 0.35–1.10 — both groups show high variance
Bad policyholders are only 1.3% of portfolio (n=433) — the half-density shape shows heavier tail risk


The raincloud plot highlights the Bad group in blue. The median difference between Bad and Good is actually modest. What the raincloud reveals is the distribution shape — the half-density for Bad policyholders is wider with a heavier upper tail, meaning more of them have high loss ratios. Both groups have similarly wide IQRs crossing break-even. The bonus-malus system identifies customers who are more likely to generate large claims, even if the average difference is not dramatic.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 8: Comprehensive Policies Cost More Per Claim
text:
Insight 8: Comprehensive Policies Cost More Per Claim


COMP/E: +Excess mean severity = €753 per claim; median = €547 — highest among all types
CC: +Add-ons mean = €651, median = €437 — moderate severity
Wide gap between mean and median across ALL types confirms heavily right-skewed distributions


Comprehensive policies generate not only more claims but also more expensive ones. COMP_E and COMP_N show wider half-density curves at higher severity levels. The large gap between the mean diamond and the median box line across all policy types confirms that a small number of very large claims drive average severity up. This unpredictability is the core source of underwriting risk.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 9: Young Drivers File Claims 2.7x More Often
text:
Insight 9: Young Drivers File Claims 2.7x More Often


19-25 group: mean frequency = 0.716 — highest of all age groups
56-65 group: mean frequency = 0.289 — safest segment
Young drivers file claims 2.5x more often than the 56-65 group (0.716 / 0.289 = 2.48x)


A lollipop chart is cleaner than a bar chart for showing this comparison — less ink, same information, the dot draws the eye straight to the value. The 19-25 group highlighted in blue stands out clearly at 0.716. Then frequency drops steadily through middle age. Young drivers file claims 2.5 times more often than the safest group. Note the 19-25 sample is relatively small as very few young drivers appear in this portfolio.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 10: Urban Inland Drivers Have Highest Claim Rates
text:
Insight 10: Urban Inland Drivers Have Highest Claim Rates


Inland Urban: mean frequency = 0.371 — highest among all combinations
Coastal Urban: 0.314 vs Coastal Rural: 0.284 — urban always higher
Urban drivers consistently file 10-25% more claims than rural across all regions


Urban drivers consistently file more claims than rural drivers across all three municipality types. Inland urban shows the highest frequency at 0.371. The blue bars are always taller than the grey bars within each municipality type. The urban vs rural gap is consistent across all regions, confirming that circulation area is a strong predictor of claim volatility.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 11: COMP_N Loss Ratio Rose to 1.17 by 2024
text:
Insight 11: COMP_N Loss Ratio Rose to 1.17 by 2024


COMP_N rose from 0.71 (2022) to 1.17 (2024) — crossed break-even in 2024
COMP_E rose from 0.64 (2022) to 1.11 (2024) — also crossed break-even
TP, TPG, CC remain below break-even — basic coverage types remain profitable


This is arguably the most alarming finding. COMP_N and COMP_E both crossed the break-even line in 2024. COMP_N went from 0.71 in 2022 to 1.17 in 2024. This means the insurer is now paying out more in claims than it collects in premiums for these policy types. This could indicate rising repair costs or medical inflation. Basic coverage types remain comfortably below break-even throughout the period.
